questions.question: Explain why trench warfare and stalemate developed on the Western Front.
questions.expected_answer: After the German advance was stopped at the Marne in September 1914 and the race to the sea, a line of trenches about seven hundred kilometres long ran from the Belgian coast to Switzerland. Machine guns, barbed wire and artillery made defence much stronger than attack, so neither side could break through: stalemate. Attempts to end it included long bombardments, poison gas first used on a large scale at Ypres in April 1915, tanks first used at the Somme in September 1916 and aircraft, but battles such as Verdun, the Somme and Passchendaele cost huge casualties for small gains until movement returned in 1918.

questions.question: Describe the layout of the trenches and the conditions soldiers faced.
questions.expected_answer: Trench systems had front-line, support and reserve trenches joined by communication trenches, dug in zigzags, with fire steps, sandbag parapets, duckboards, dugouts and barbed wire, facing the enemy across no man's land. Conditions included mud and water, trench foot, rats, lice and trench fever, terrible smells and cold tinned food. Routine included stand-to at dawn and dusk, work, night patrols and raids, boredom and sudden terror, and units were rotated. Shell shock, psychological trauma now recognised as post-traumatic stress, was often treated as weakness or cowardice.

questions.question: Explain how songs and poetry are useful sources about the war.
questions.expected_answer: Songs such as It's a Long Way to Tipperary, Pack Up Your Troubles and Keep the Home Fires Burning, and soldiers' parody songs, show humour, coping and attitudes hidden by propaganda. Rupert Brooke's patriotic The Soldier of 1914 was written before he saw the trenches; John McCrae's In Flanders Fields of 1915 made the poppy a symbol of remembrance; Sassoon and Owen, whose Dulce et Decorum Est describes a gas attack and calls the patriotic Latin phrase the old lie, show anger later in the war. Historians ask who, when, why and for whom, and compare sources, since attitudes varied.
